scope.end: 12b: the Gemara extends Rav Mari's 'like the gazelle and the hart' to R. Shimon (12b.1)

sections.title: Mishnah: Which Animals Cannot Redeem a Peter Chamor, and R. Eliezer's Hybrid
sections.gist: A list of animals unfit to redeem a *peter chamor* (firstborn donkey). R. Eliezer allows the sheep-goat hybrid but not the *koy*, and a *kohen* given the donkey itself may keep it only after designating a lamb in its place.

bullets.text: A *peter chamor* (firstborn donkey) may not be redeemed with a calf, a wild animal, a slaughtered animal, a *tereifah*, a sheep-goat hybrid (*kil'ayim*), or a *koy*, an animal of uncertain domestic or wild status.
R. Eliezer permits the hybrid, because it is a lamb (*seh*). He forbids the *koy*, because its status is uncertain.
If the owner gave the *peter chamor* itself to a *kohen*, the *kohen* may not keep it until he designates a lamb in its place.

sections.title: Ben Bag Bag's Seh–Seh from the Pesach, Limited by 'Tifdeh, Tifdeh'
sections.gist: The Mishnah's exclusions follow ben Bag Bag's *gezeirah shavah* from the Pesach, while the doubled 'you shall redeem' admits female, blemished and older lambs.

bullets.text: The first clause of the Mishnah is ben Bag Bag's. "*Seh*" is said of redeeming the *peter chamor* (Shemot 13:13) and of the Pesach (Shemot 12:3). Just as the Pesach excludes all the animals on the list, so does redemption.
Challenge: then, like the Pesach, the lamb should also have to be male, unblemished and in its first year (Shemot 12:5).
Answer: "*tifdeh*" (Shemot 13:13) and "*tifdeh*" (Shemot 34:20). The repetition includes a female, a blemished lamb and one past its first year.
Challenge: if the repetition includes, it should include the Mishnah's list as well. Answer: then the *gezeirah shavah* of *seh–seh* would serve no purpose.

sections.title: Borderline Lambs: Ben Pekua, a Lookalike, Redeemed Pesulei Ha'mukdashin
sections.gist: Three questions on what else may redeem a *peter chamor*, each framed by one tanna's view: a *ben pekua*, a lamb that resembles another species, and a redeemed disqualified consecrated animal.

bullets.text: Each question opens by setting aside the view on which there is nothing to ask, then asks according to the other view.

chart.caption: The three questions about borderline lambs
rows: The Rabbis: its mother's *shechitah* permits it
R. Meir: it needs its own *shechitah*, so it is a full lamb
Meat in the pot, or a lamb that runs about
Mar Zutra: may not redeem. Rav Ashi: may
The Rabbis, who forbid a hybrid
R. Eliezer, who permits even a hybrid
Only a true hybrid is excluded, or a *nidmeh* too
R. Yehuda: benefit from a *peter chamor* is forbidden
R. Shimon: benefit is permitted, so nothing passes to the lamb
The donkey's status cannot take hold (*ein issur chal al issur*), or redemption merely removes it
Rav Mari: "like the gazelle and the hart" excludes them, even for R. Shimon

sections.continues: The series of questions continues on 12b with an animal bought with *Shevi'it* produce.

children.title: Ben Pekua: Meat in the Pot or a Running Lamb? Mar Zutra vs. Rav Ashi
children.gist: For the Rabbis, a fetus permitted by its mother's *shechitah* might count as slaughtered. Mar Zutra forbids it and Rav Ashi permits it, and they argue over how far ben Bag Bag's derivation reaches.

bullets.text: Question: may one redeem with a *ben pekua*? R. Meir requires its own *shechitah*, so for him it is a full lamb. The question is for the Rabbis, for whom its mother's *shechitah* permits it.
Is it like meat placed in a pot, and so a slaughtered animal? Or, since it now runs about, is it called a lamb?
Mar Zutra: one may not redeem with it. Rav Ashi: one may.
Rav Ashi: if your reason is the analogy to the Pesach, for which a *ben pekua* is unfit, then require a male, unblemished, first-year lamb as well. Mar Zutra: "*tifdeh, tifdeh*" includes those.
Rav Ashi: then "*tifdeh, tifdeh*" includes a *ben pekua* too. Mar Zutra: then what would the *seh–seh* analogy be for?

children.title: A Nidmeh: Is a Lookalike Lamb Like a Hybrid for the Rabbis?
children.gist: For the Rabbis, who forbid a hybrid, does a lamb born of sheep but resembling another species count as one too? Two *baraitot* are tested, a cow's goat-like offspring and Rabba bar Shmuel's definition, and neither settles it.

bullets.text: For R. Eliezer there is no question: he permits even a true hybrid, so all the more a sheep's offspring that merely looks like a goat.
For the Rabbis: do they forbid only a hybrid and permit a *nidmeh*, or is there no difference between them?

children.title: A Cow's Goat-Like Offspring: Rabbis' View, or Follow the Mother?
children.gist: A *baraita* bars a cow's goat-like offspring, implying a ewe's is allowed. The Gemara assigns it to R. Eliezer, teaching that one follows the mother.

bullets.text: *Baraita*: a cow that gave birth to a goat of sorts: one may not redeem with it. By inference, a ewe's goat-like offspring may be used.
That inference is useless for R. Eliezer, who permits even a hybrid, so the *baraita* must be the Rabbis'. They would then permit a *nidmeh*.
Deflected: it is R. Eliezer's, and it teaches that one does not follow the offspring's appearance but its mother. The cow's offspring is a calf, which cannot redeem.

illustration.caption: The *baraita* on a goat-like offspring, read as R. Eliezer's: the offspring follows its mother, so a cow's is a calf and a ewe's is a lamb (Bekhorot 12a).

children.title: Rabba bar Shmuel's Baraita: Offerings, Bekhor, Ma'aser or Redemption?
children.gist: A *baraita* treats a *nidmeh* like a hybrid. Offerings, firstborn status and tithe seem already covered, so it seems to be about redemption, until the Gemara finds it a point about tithe.

bullets.text: Rabba bar Shmuel's *baraita*: what is a hybrid? A ewe that bore a goat of sorts, whose father is a lamb. The Gemara: with a lamb for a father it is only a *nidmeh*. So read: what is like a hybrid, and was equated with one by the Rabbis?
For which law? Not offerings: Vayikra 22:27 already excludes a *nidmeh* ("or a goat") in the same verse that excludes a hybrid.
Not firstborn status: "But the firstborn of an ox" (Bamidbar 18:17) requires an ox whose firstborn is an ox.
Not animal tithe: the *gezeirah shavah* of "under" (Vayikra 22:27 and 27:32) already applies the offerings rule. So it must mean redeeming the *peter chamor*, and a *nidmeh* is unfit.

Deflected: it is about tithe, for a *nidmeh* with some features of its mother. One might have learned from "passing", said of both tithe and the firstborn, that just as such an animal is a firstborn (see 16b), it is tithed. The *baraita* teaches that "under" governs instead.
So the *baraita* proves nothing about redeeming the donkey.

chart.caption: Where could Rabba bar Shmuel's *baraita* apply?
rows: Yes, in the end: a *nidmeh* with some of its mother's features, which "passing" might have included

children.title: Redeemed Pesulei Ha'mukdashin: Ein Issur Chal Al Issur, or 'Like the Gazelle'?
children.gist: For R. Yehuda, can the donkey's forbidden status pass to a lamb already forbidden for shearing and work? Rav Mari answers from 'like the gazelle and the hart', which excludes such animals even for R. Shimon.

bullets.text: Question: may one redeem with *pesulei ha'mukdashin* that were redeemed? Such animals remain forbidden for shearing and work. Does *ein issur chal al issur* apply?

For R. Shimon there is no question: he permits benefit from a *peter chamor*, so it is non-sacred and no forbidden status passes to the lamb. The question is for R. Yehuda, who forbids benefit from it.
One side: redemption must transfer the donkey's forbidden status to the lamb. It cannot take hold on a lamb that is already forbidden.
Other side: the lamb is permitted after redemption anyway. So redemption merely removes the donkey's status and transfers nothing, and the principle does not apply.

Rav Mari, son of Rav Kahana: the Torah calls these animals "like the gazelle and like the hart" (Devarim 12:15, *ka'tzvi ve'kha'ayal*). A gazelle or hart cannot redeem a *peter chamor*, so neither can they.
The Gemara: on this reasoning, even R. Shimon would bar them, for the same verse applies to him.

key_terms.definition: The firstborn male of a donkey, which its owner must redeem by giving a lamb (seh) to a kohen, or else break its neck.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks which animals may serve as the lamb that redeems it, and what the kohen may do if given the donkey itself.

key_terms.definition: A method of derivation that applies a law from one passage to another because the same word appears in both.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Ben Bag Bag's seh–seh analogy to the Pesach rules out the Mishnah's list, and "under" and "passing" are weighed for the animal tithe.

key_terms.definition: An animal born of two different species, here a cross between a sheep and a goat.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Rabbis forbid redeeming a firstborn donkey with it; R. Eliezer permits it as a seh.

key_terms.sense: a fetus found alive in a slaughtered animal
key_terms.definition: A live fetus taken from its mother after she was ritually slaughtered. The Rabbis hold that the mother's shechitah permits it; R. Meir requires it to be slaughtered on its own.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Mar Zutra forbids redeeming with it, treating it as slaughtered meat; Rav Ashi permits it, since it runs about as a lamb.

key_terms.definition: An animal born of parents of one species whose appearance is that of a different species.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara asks whether the Rabbis, who bar a hybrid, bar a nidmeh too; two baraitot are tested and deflected.

key_terms.sense: blemished consecrated animals that were redeemed
key_terms.definition: Consecrated animals that became disqualified, usually by a blemish, and were redeemed. They may be eaten like non-sacred meat, but shearing and working them remain forbidden.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Mari learns from "like the gazelle and the hart" that they cannot redeem a firstborn donkey.

key_terms.sense: one prohibition cannot take hold where another exists
key_terms.definition: The principle that a second prohibition does not take effect on an object or act already subject to an existing prohibition.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The question is whether it blocks the donkey's forbidden status from passing to an already-forbidden redeemed consecrated lamb.

judgment_calls: The three questions (ben pekua, nidmeh, redeemed pesulei ha'mukdashin) are grouped under one parent because they share the question of what else may redeem; each could have stood as its own top-level section.
The ben Bag Bag derivation (s2) is kept separate from the Mishnah rather than nested under it, since it is the Gemara's source discussion and its terms recur in the ben pekua debate.
Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita (s7) could have been split into two children, the four-way elimination and the deflection about tithe; kept as one because the deflection simply answers the elimination.
coverage_notes: No shiur for this daf; the whole outline is built from the Gemara text.
The previous daf's essay tail covers the final Mishnah of the previous perek (11b), which lies before this outline's scope.

Scope ends at 12b.1, the close of the pesulei ha'mukdashin question. The rest of 12b (the Shevi'it-produce question, Rav Chisda, the kohen given the donkey, the Mishnah on the lamb that died, and redemption timing) belongs to the next outline.
Sefaria's 'prohibits' and 'permitted' in the Mishnah are rendered as 'forbidden' and 'permitted' throughout.
